name: @nifdi/mcp

tools.name: get_diagram
tools.description: Read the diagram as nifdi XML — the complete, authoritative model, and the canonical shape to mimic when writing XML back with set_diagram or insert. Accepted set_diagram shorthands are normalized here, so use this output as the source of truth; do not add a version attribute when authoring MCP XML. Blocks carry pos="x y" and size="w h" (space-separated numbers, both optional on input — omitted geometry is completed by the server; this output always shows the resolved values) plus named style classes defined in a <style> block; that style block uses semicolon-separated nifdi semantic declarations (fill-colour: #fff; border-colour: #000;), not CSS fill/stroke/color. Comma-separated declarations are accepted only for legacy XML compatibility. Attached labels are nested elements carrying place (and gap) instead of pos, for example <icon asset="aws:amazon-ec2"><text>Amazon EC2</text></icon> for the default caption below the icon, or <text place="on top-edge"> under a container for a title astride its border; a container child without place is contained as usual. Containers nest their children directly (a <container> holds its <container>/<text>/<icon> children — there is no nested <canvas>). A <path> wires two blocks through <from> and <to> child elements (each with a block id and a side), plus an optional space-separated numeric `segments` attribute — not SVG path syntax. A connector's label is a <text> (or <container>) child of that <path>. The diagram's source (e.g. Mermaid) is included when present. Pass format "svg" for a self-contained augmented SVG with rendered shapes and embedded asset content, suitable for saving as a .nifdi.svg file. Neither format is a picture — to look at the diagram, call render_diagram.

diagramId.description: The diagram to act on: an id from create_diagram or list_diagrams, or a pasted URL of the diagram's editor page, which spells the same id. Required on every call — this server keeps no current diagram between calls.

tools.name: render_diagram
tools.description: See the diagram: renders it to a PNG and returns the picture, so you can look at what you have built instead of inferring it from XML. This is a screenshot of the real thing — nifdi's own renderer draws it, the same way the live editor and the saved .nifdi.svg file do — so drop-shadows, rounded borders, markers and icon artwork are all as they will be. Use it to check what only a picture can tell you: overall layout, what overlaps or collides, whether a label landed on the host you meant, where a connector routed, how the colours read. Cheap and read-only — render after building the first blocks, after each batch of edits, and once before you call a diagram finished, then fix what you see. Do not convert the SVG with an external rasterizer instead; those drop the effects nifdi relies on. Reports the pixel size, the diagram's own size and the scale used, plus a note for any artwork shown as a placeholder.

diagramId.description: The diagram to act on: an id from create_diagram or list_diagrams, or a pasted URL of the diagram's editor page, which spells the same id. Required on every call — this server keeps no current diagram between calls.

width.description: target image width in pixels. Omitted, the diagram is drawn at twice its own size, which keeps label text legible. Held between 64 and 1568 pixels on the longest edge whatever is asked for, so a big diagram comes back scaled to fit and the result says what it did. Ask for more only to read fine detail on a large diagram.

tools.name: set_diagram
tools.description:
Replace the diagram with nifdi XML — the complete, authoritative model. For partial construction prefer insert + connect + set_style; use set_diagram when replacing the whole diagram. This is a clean replace: blocks, paths, title and source are taken verbatim from the XML. Blocks carry pos="x y" and size="w h", both optional — geometry may be omitted or approximate and the server completes and repairs it, the same as insert; a version attribute is not required. Standard shape is <diagram><title/><canvas/><style/></diagram>, but tolerant input also accepts direct diagram children as implicit canvas content, root title="...", endpoint side="...", and bare or # block ids. get_diagram returns the canonical normalized result. Label a connector by nesting the label inside its <path> — with no pos/size, so nifdi places it on the line and keeps it there when the path re-routes:
  <path><from block="#a" attach="right"/><to block="#b" attach="left"/><text>Transformed data</text></path>
Plain nifdi XML cannot carry new asset content: an <assets> block in XML is ignored, and icons must reference assets already in the store by id (unknown asset ids render as placeholders). To upload icons or background images, pass a full augmented .nifdi.svg document instead — its embedded asset content is uploaded to the diagram's asset store. To adjust a diagram to match a source language while preserving styling and manual layout, use set_source instead. Parse diagnostics are reported in the result.

xml.description:
Complete nifdi XML. pos/size are optional on every block — the server completes and repairs omitted geometry. A declared pos arranges blocks against one another rather than fixing canvas coordinates, and the result says where each block landed. A declared size that a block's own contents plus their margins overflow lands on that floor instead, and the result says what landed — to go smaller, shrink the contents first (a label's margin or font-size, an icon's size). Root it however the content falls: <canvas>, a single block, several blocks side by side, or any wrapper element. An <icon> must carry an asset reference: asset="#asset-…" for an asset already in the diagram (from get_diagram) or registered with add_asset, or asset="library:name" for an installed library icon found with search_icons.
LABELS — nest the element inside its host: a bare <text> inside <icon> (for example <icon asset="aws:amazon-ec2"><text>Amazon EC2</text></icon>) is the default below-icon caption; name the side for any other, e.g. <icon asset="aws:amazon-ec2"><text place="right-edge">Amazon EC2</text></icon> for a label to the right. A place attribute (place="right-edge", place="on top-edge", place="top-left-corner", …) selects any other placement. A container's label is nested the same way — <container class="zone"><text>Web Server</text></container> sizes to fit it. Text sitting beside, above or below an icon in a picture you are recreating is that icon's label: nest it, and never write a separate sibling text block next to one, which nifdi cannot then keep in place. A <text>'s words are markdown, one line per line of the block: <container class="zone"><text>**Web tier**
- nginx
- node</text></container> is one block of three lines, a bold title over two bullets. Indentation you give the lines for readability is removed.
STYLE — a <style> block counts wherever you write it, and speaks the full set_style selector language, descendant and child selectors included (`.azureBox text { text-colour: #ffffff }`), and its property names and values are set_style's own: canonical longhands such as `icon-colour`, `text-alignment`, `shadow-colour` and `marker-end-width`, written as `property: value;` with semicolons (commas only for legacy XML compatibility). Old short leaves remain load-compatible, and a name or value neither grammar can use is reported rather than dropped. A text property written on a container styles the text inside it.
CLASSES — a class name is a group that survives the round trip: the elements carrying it come back carrying it, and `set_style ".name { … }"` later reaches exactly them. A name with no rule in this fragment is kept as a group to style in a later call. A block naming a class the diagram already carries joins it and arrives styled by its declarations — unless this fragment redeclares the name, which then speaks alone for its own blocks. A text inserted inside a member of a styled class takes that class's text styling. The result says which classes joined and what was applied.

tools.name: normalize_diagram
tools.description: Preflight nifdi XML before set_diagram: parse tolerant nifdi XML, report diagnostics, and return canonical normalized XML (with any omitted pos/size filled in) without editing the diagram. Asset references (asset="#asset-…") are resolved against the named diagram's store. Useful before set_diagram to check accepted shorthands such as root title attributes, implicit canvas content, endpoint side attributes, bare ids, omitted pos/size on any block, nested below-icon captions with no pos/size (<icon asset="aws:amazon-ec2"><text>Label</text></icon>), and legacy comma style declarations.

tools.name: connect
tools.description:
Add connectors, each named end to end: `connections` is a list of {from, to} pairs and every pair becomes one routed connector pointing from→to, so the direction and the pairing are exactly what you wrote — a fan-out is several pairs sharing a `from`. Each end joins a block, which lets routing choose the side, or one side of it (`attach`), the same distinction as a <path>'s <from attach="right"/> in get_diagram. A pair is always added, even between blocks that are already joined, so two connectors can run between the same blocks; the summary says when one did.
STYLE — a connector you do not style takes the look the diagram's connectors share (its `path {}` rule, which set_style `path { … }` sets for every connector, including later ones). `style` styles every connector this call creates; a connection's own `style` styles that one and wins over `style` where both set a property. Both take set_style's path declarations and are kept on the connectors they name, so they never become the diagram's shared connector look.
The result's `pathIds` lines up with `connections`, one id per pair, or null for a pair that could not be routed (the summary names it). Label a connector with set_text on its path id, or author the label inline in XML as a <text> child of the <path>: <path><from block="#a" attach="right"/><to block="#b" attach="left"/><text>Transformed data</text></path>

block.description: id of the block this end joins (the '#' prefix is optional)

attach.description: pin this end to one side of the block. Omit it to join the block itself, and routing picks the side — and picks again whenever the block moves. Pin a side only when the picture needs that side

from.description: one end of a connector, e.g. {block: "#api"} or {block: "#api", attach: "right"}

block.description: id of the block this end joins (the '#' prefix is optional)

attach.description: pin this end to one side of the block. Omit it to join the block itself, and routing picks the side — and picks again whenever the block moves. Pin a side only when the picture needs that side

to.description: one end of a connector, e.g. {block: "#api"} or {block: "#api", attach: "right"}

style.description: Style for this connector alone, over the shared `style`: `property: value;` declarations with no selector or braces, e.g. "path-colour: #64748b; line-style: dashed; marker-end: dart". PATH props: path-colour, path-width, line-style (solid|dashed), line-repeat-distance, path-corner-radius, clearance, path-margin, marker-start, marker-end (`<style> [width] [length] [gap]` or `none`; styles triangle, dart, square-chevron, round-chevron, clipped-chevron, flat-chevron, chamfer, square-cap, round-cap, circle, ring) and their marker-start-*/marker-end-* longhands.

connections.description: the connectors to add, e.g. [{from: {block: "#web"}, to: {block: "#api", attach: "left"}}]

style.description: Style for every connector this call creates: `property: value;` declarations with no selector or braces, e.g. "path-colour: #64748b; line-style: dashed; marker-end: dart". PATH props: path-colour, path-width, line-style (solid|dashed), line-repeat-distance, path-corner-radius, clearance, path-margin, marker-start, marker-end (`<style> [width] [length] [gap]` or `none`; styles triangle, dart, square-chevron, round-chevron, clipped-chevron, flat-chevron, chamfer, square-cap, round-cap, circle, ring) and their marker-start-*/marker-end-* longhands.

tools.name: delete
tools.description: Delete blocks and connectors, re-routing the survivors. `ids` takes both kinds, mixed freely in one list — a connector's id (from connect or get_diagram) deletes that connector, a block's id deletes that block, and the '#' prefix is optional on either. Deleting a block takes its contents, its attached labels and every connector wired to it with it; `keepContents` keeps a container's children and removes only the container itself. The result names everything that went, the cascade included, so it does not cost a get_diagram to find out. An id nothing in the diagram has is skipped and reported (deleting what is already gone is not an error); a call where no id names anything fails.

ids.description: ids of blocks and/or connectors to delete, in any mix

keepContents.description: delete a named container but keep its children, which stay in the diagram

diagramId.description: The diagram to act on: an id from create_diagram or list_diagrams, or a pasted URL of the diagram's editor page, which spells the same id. Required on every call — this server keeps no current diagram between calls.

tools.name: align
tools.description: Align blocks to a shared edge or centre line. The named blocks are grouped into bands across the alignment axis — rows for left/centre/right, columns for top/middle/bottom — and each band moves as a unit to the extreme edge (or centre) of the group as it stands, so blocks sharing a band keep their relative positions instead of converging onto the same edge. Blocks not named are left alone but may be pushed aside. The result says which blocks actually moved. To spread blocks out evenly rather than line them up, use arrange with distributeHorizontally / distributeVertically.

diagramId.description: The diagram to act on: an id from create_diagram or list_diagrams, or a pasted URL of the diagram's editor page, which spells the same id. Required on every call — this server keeps no current diagram between calls.

tools.name: arrange
tools.description: Rearrange blocks as a group. "distributeHorizontally" / "distributeVertically" give the blocks equal gaps along that axis, leaving the two outermost where they are and keeping their current order — the way to even out a row or column of stages. "flipHorizontal" / "flipVertical" mirror their positions about the group's centre line (and swap which side connectors leave from); "transpose" swaps the two axes. The result says which blocks actually moved.

tools.name: set_style
tools.description:
Apply a nifdi style sheet to the diagram, with reflow physics. `style` is CSS-like: one or more `selector { property: value; ... }` rules, the same canonical semicolon grammar as the <style> block in get_diagram/insert (commas are accepted only for legacy XML compatibility). **Every property name, per element type, is on the `style` parameter below.**
ONE VOCABULARY — this grammar and a <style> block accept the same property names and the same values, so a declaration that works in one works in the other. Canonical longhands are globally unique: use `icon-colour`, `text-alignment`, `shadow-std-deviation`, `marker-end-width`. A property or value the element cannot take is named and skipped by both, never silently dropped — and the skip names the property that would have worked, so guessing costs one call rather than a read-back.
SELECTORS — target anything: `#id` (a specific block or path), a type (`container`, `text`, `icon`, `path`), `.class` (every element get_diagram shows carrying that class), or `canvas`. Comma-group them to style a mixed selection at once, and descendant/child selectors work as in CSS — both spelled out on the `style` parameter. A rule narrower than a bare type rule keeps its values on the elements it named: they are not folded into the type rule on the next read, and a block inserted afterwards does not inherit them. Later rules win. Colours are hex like #aabbcc.
TEXT INSIDE — a text property written on a container, an icon or a path styles the text inside it, as CSS does for inheritable properties: `.titleText { font-weight: 700 }` is applied as `.titleText text { font-weight: 700 }`, and the result says so. Direct application always wins, so `icon-colour` on an icon is still its tint. `canvas` does not cascade — every text on the canvas is `text { ... }`.
Returns the resolved attributes applied (with the ids each landed on) and any skipped declarations.

tools.name: copy_style
tools.description: Copy style attributes from one block onto others, with reflow physics. By default copies all applicable style; pass `categories` to copy only those (same category names as set_style). Attributes that don't apply to a target's type are skipped and reported. Text content is not style — use set_text for that.

tools.name: set_text
tools.description:
Set text content with reflow physics. WITHOUT `place` this is what typing on the target does: a text block sets its content; a container or intersection sets its immediate child text, creating that text inside it when it has none; an icon sets its caption, creating one below it when it has none. WITH `place` it addresses an attachment site on the named host instead, and touches nothing else there — so `place: "top-left-corner"` on a captioned icon adds a badge rather than moving the caption. A corner or `<edge>` site holds one attachment: text already there has its content set where it stands, an empty site gets a new label, and a site held by something carrying no text is refused, naming the occupant. An `on <edge>`/`outside <edge>` site is unlimited, so it always creates. To MOVE an existing label, name that text's own id (get_diagram carries it) with the `place` to move it to and no `content` — it keeps its words. A container's contained text sits at no site, so `place` on a container titles its border beside whatever it already holds. The result names what each id took — set, created, refused or skipped — and a create that lands beside an existing label names that label, so a second attachment is never mistaken for a move.
A path id sets that connector's label, creating it if the connector has none and updating it if it has one. The label rides the connector and re-places itself when the path re-routes.
This is also the repair for a label authored the wrong way round: if a free text block is already sitting beside, above or below an icon, delete it and set_text the icon with place naming that side, so the label becomes the icon's and moves with it.
Content is markdown (see `content`): one block holds a whole note or caption, so never spread its lines across several text blocks.

content.description: The words to set, as markdown — the same syntax a person types in the editor: a newline is a new line of the same block, `# `/`## `/`### ` open a heading line, `- ` and `1. ` make list items (two leading spaces nest one), **bold**, _italic_ and `code` mark runs, and a ``` line before and after holds a code block. Omit it, with `place`, to move the label ids name without changing its words; a call with neither content nor place is refused.

place.description: Where on the host the text goes, in the attachment placement grammar: `<corner>` ("top-left-corner"), `<edge>` — the abbreviation of `outside-middle <edge>` — ("bottom-edge", the default caption; "right-edge"), `on <edge>` ("on top-edge", astride the border) or `outside <edge>` ("outside bottom-edge", clear of it). Corners and `<edge>` are one-per-site; `on`/`outside` sites are unlimited. This is not insert's `where` grammar: `where`'s `end` and `relation: "inside"` resolve once at insert time and manage nothing afterwards. On a connector or its label the path-label grammar applies instead — `<on|outside>? midpoint <left|right|above|below>?`, e.g. "on midpoint" (the default, breaking the stroke) or "outside midpoint above" (beside the line; the side is relative to the hosting run's axis).

tools.name: resize
tools.description: Resize blocks to an explicit size, with reflow physics: contents keep their padding, neighbours are pushed aside, and paths re-route. `width`/`height` set the size absolutely; `dWidth`/`dHeight` adjust relatively. Omitted axes keep their current size; blocks grow/shrink toward the bottom-right. Icons are square — one axis is enough. Text blocks are not resizable here: set the wrap-width style instead. A block cannot go smaller than its own contents plus their margins: an axis asked below that floor lands on it, and the result says what landed. To go smaller, shrink the contents first — a label's margin or font-size, an icon's size.

diagramId.description: The diagram to act on: an id from create_diagram or list_diagrams, or a pasted URL of the diagram's editor page, which spells the same id. Required on every call — this server keeps no current diagram between calls.

tools.name: move
tools.description:
Move blocks, either by a delta or to a named destination — give `dx`/`dy` or `where`, never both.
`dx`/`dy` nudges: either one on its own is enough, the omitted axis is zero, so `dy: 40` moves straight down. Neighbours are pushed aside, and the blocks stay in whatever container they are already in however far you push them — that container grows to keep hold of them rather than letting them escape. A nudge never changes what a block belongs to. Physics can absorb part of a delta; when what landed differs from what was asked for, the result says so per block.
`where` relocates: it names where the blocks should end up, in the same drop-target vocabulary insert uses — {block, anchor, relation?, end?} (e.g. {block: "#zone", relation: "inside"} to put them in a container, {block: "#db", anchor: "right-edge"} to put them beside one), {between: [id1, id2]}, or omit `where`'s fields and pass {} to append below existing canvas content. Room is made at the destination for the blocks' combined footprint and they are re-nested there, so this is the way to restructure. `where` may not name a block being moved, or one inside it.

where.description: Where to place the content relative to existing blocks — either {block, anchor, relation?, end?} (e.g. {block: "#db", anchor: "right-edge"} for beside, {block: "#db", anchor: "top-edge", end: "left"} for above at the left end, {block: "#zone", relation: "inside", anchor: "top-left-corner"} for into a container's corner, {block: "#zone", relation: "inside"} for centred in a container) or {between: [id1, id2]}. Omit to append below existing canvas content. Every anchor clears the sides it names by the two blocks' own margins, so spacing matches the rest of the diagram: an edge places the content beside that edge and centred on it, a corner places it diagonally clear of both sides it names, and naming no anchor at all centres it (which is why that needs relation "inside"; to sit beside a block, name an edge or a corner). This is one-shot drop-target vocabulary, not the enduring placement grammar, despite the shared edge and corner spellings: `end` resolves to a coordinate at insert time and manages nothing afterwards (the placement grammar has no edge-ends — a place attribute naming one is read leniently, with the end dropped and a warning). To attach content to a host rather than drop it near one, nest it under that host with place. Whatever this resolves to, the echo answers in the same frame get_diagram uses: a fragment that lands inside a container comes back nested inside it, and every pos is measured from the element enclosing it, never from the canvas. Those enclosing containers are marked existing="true" — they were already there, this insert did not make them, and they are stubs carrying geometry alone, so their own classes, labels and other children are not listed.

block.description: id of an existing block to place relative to (the '#' prefix from path refs is optional); pair with anchor and optionally relation/end

relation.description: whether the content lands within the block or beyond its border; defaults to outside. "inside" means containment, so it requires a container and errors on an icon or a text

anchor.description: a named edge or corner of the block. An edge centres the content on that edge unless an end is given; a corner names two sides and places the content diagonally clear of both. Omit it, with relation "inside", to centre the content in the block — naming no side is what centred means, which is why it is only available inside. Every gap comes from the two blocks' margins, never a fixed number

end.description: position along an edge anchor: left/right for top-edge and bottom-edge, top/bottom for left-edge and right-edge. Omit for centred; corners take no end

between.description: ids of exactly two existing blocks; the content lands centred in the gap between them. An alternative to block/relation/anchor/end, not a companion — naming both is an error

diagramId.description: The diagram to act on: an id from create_diagram or list_diagrams, or a pasted URL of the diagram's editor page, which spells the same id. Required on every call — this server keeps no current diagram between calls.

tools.name: set_background
tools.description: Set a container's background: an image, a solid colour, or cleared. This paints one block. The page behind the diagram is not a container and is not reachable here — style it with set_style `canvas { fill-colour: #ffffff; pattern-type: none }`, where pattern-type none clears the dot grid a new diagram starts with. For an image, pass the asset reference from add_asset (or get_diagram); the image cover-scales to fill the container, clipped to its shape (including corner radius), and moves with it. `crop` [x0 y0 x1 y1] in image pixels selects the visible viewport of the image; it defaults to the whole image. The image is not a separate block — it is part of the container, and clears when the container is deleted.

clear.description: pass true to remove the background

background.description: Exactly one of `asset` (+ optional `crop`), `colour`, or `clear: true`.

tools.name: search_icons
tools.description: Search the installed icon libraries (aws (installs on first use), azure (installs on first use), generic, google-cloud (installs on first use), iconoir (installs on first use)) for official product and concept artwork. A library that is not installed yet is installed on first use and then served from local disk; one this server cannot install says so. Returns matches with a `ref` like "aws:amazon-ec2" to use directly as the asset attribute of an <icon> in insert or set_diagram; the artwork and its licence provenance are copied into the diagram on use, so the saved file stays self-contained. Try product names ("EC2", "Cloud SQL"), concepts ("database", "user", "queue") or category words. Terms are matched loosely and ranked by how much of the query an icon covers, so an extra or unofficial word narrows the ranking rather than emptying the result — `note` names any term nothing matched at all. `library` is a preference, not a filter: the search always runs across every library, in-library matches come back in `results` and the rest in `otherLibraries`, so a scoped query never comes back empty without telling you the answer was elsewhere. Prefer these over fetching icons externally — use add_asset only for artwork no library covers.

query.description: words to match against icon names and categories; all optional, best coverage wins

library.description: prefer one library, e.g. "aws" — matches elsewhere still come back, in otherLibraries

tools.name: add_asset
tools.description:
Register an SVG icon or raster image in the diagram's asset store, returning the reference to use in <icon asset="…"> (insert / set_diagram) or set_background. `content` is either SVG text (sanitized server-side: scripts and external references are stripped; max 1MB) or a base64 data URI for PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP (max 5MB). Icons should be square. The asset is stored content-addressed, so re-adding the same content is idempotent and returns the same reference.
Prefer search_icons first — the bundled AWS/Azure/GCP/Iconoir libraries cover most product icons with official artwork and need no fetching. For anything else, fetch the SVG yourself (with your own web tools) and pass it here; this server never fetches, so nothing about the workspace leaves the machine. Good sources: the Iconify API serves plain SVG at https://api.iconify.design/{prefix}/{name}.svg (e.g. simple-icons for brand logos, logos for coloured product marks); include provenance for whatever you fetch. Assets left unreferenced by any block are garbage-collected when the server restarts, so add and use them in the same session.

content.description: SVG text, or data:image/png;base64,… for raster images

provenance.description: Attribution for the artwork. Strongly encouraged for fetched content: it is embedded in the saved file so the diagram stays licence-clean. Omit it only when the origin is genuinely unknown.

tools.name: insert
tools.description:
Insert a fragment of nifdi XML — one or more blocks, optionally nested, with style classes. Use connect for paths and set_style for styling afterwards, and reserve set_diagram for full replacement. **Everything about the fragment itself — its shape, geometry attributes, <style> block and class names — is on the `xml` parameter; the placement vocabulary is on `where`.**
GEOMETRY — may be omitted or approximate; the server completes and repairs it: containers grow to fit their contents, declared left/right/above/below arrangement is kept, overlaps are separated, and gaps are normalised to margins. Omitting all geometry yields a vertical stack.
IDS — name blocks with id="…" and those ids are kept, so the next connect/set_style/set_text call can use them without reading the diagram back. insert only ever adds: naming an id some block already has does NOT replace or update it — the new block is inserted under a generated id instead, and the substitution is reported. To change a block you already have, use set_text/set_style/move/resize on its id, or delete it first.
<container>, <text> and <icon> are placed; <path> and other elements are skipped (the blocks still insert; wire paths up afterwards with connect, then label a connector with set_text on the new path's id). Omit `where` (or pass {}) to append below existing canvas content — the only option on an empty diagram, where an unstyled container gets a visible default outline. Style attributes the fragment leaves unspecified inherit the most common *unscoped* value among existing elements of the same type, never one scoped to a class, an id or a selector. The resolved XML is returned wearing the class names get_diagram will show, inside the existing="true" containers it landed in.

xml.description:
Fragment XML. pos/size are optional on every block — the server completes and repairs omitted geometry. A declared pos arranges blocks against one another rather than fixing canvas coordinates, and the result says where each block landed. A declared size that a block's own contents plus their margins overflow lands on that floor instead, and the result says what landed — to go smaller, shrink the contents first (a label's margin or font-size, an icon's size). Root it however the content falls: <canvas>, a single block, several blocks side by side, or any wrapper element. An <icon> must carry an asset reference: asset="#asset-…" for an asset already in the diagram (from get_diagram) or registered with add_asset, or asset="library:name" for an installed library icon found with search_icons.
LABELS — nest the element inside its host: a bare <text> inside <icon> (for example <icon asset="aws:amazon-ec2"><text>Amazon EC2</text></icon>) is the default below-icon caption; name the side for any other, e.g. <icon asset="aws:amazon-ec2"><text place="right-edge">Amazon EC2</text></icon> for a label to the right. A place attribute (place="right-edge", place="on top-edge", place="top-left-corner", …) selects any other placement. A container's label is nested the same way — <container class="zone"><text>Web Server</text></container> sizes to fit it. Text sitting beside, above or below an icon in a picture you are recreating is that icon's label: nest it, and never write a separate sibling text block next to one, which nifdi cannot then keep in place. A <text>'s words are markdown, one line per line of the block: <container class="zone"><text>**Web tier**
- nginx
- node</text></container> is one block of three lines, a bold title over two bullets. Indentation you give the lines for readability is removed.
STYLE — a <style> block counts wherever you write it, and speaks the full set_style selector language, descendant and child selectors included (`.azureBox text { text-colour: #ffffff }`), and its property names and values are set_style's own: canonical longhands such as `icon-colour`, `text-alignment`, `shadow-colour` and `marker-end-width`, written as `property: value;` with semicolons (commas only for legacy XML compatibility). Old short leaves remain load-compatible, and a name or value neither grammar can use is reported rather than dropped. A text property written on a container styles the text inside it.
CLASSES — a class name is a group that survives the round trip: the elements carrying it come back carrying it, and `set_style ".name { … }"` later reaches exactly them. A name with no rule in this fragment is kept as a group to style in a later call. A block naming a class the diagram already carries joins it and arrives styled by its declarations — unless this fragment redeclares the name, which then speaks alone for its own blocks. A text inserted inside a member of a styled class takes that class's text styling. The result says which classes joined and what was applied.

where.description: Where to place the content relative to existing blocks — either {block, anchor, relation?, end?} (e.g. {block: "#db", anchor: "right-edge"} for beside, {block: "#db", anchor: "top-edge", end: "left"} for above at the left end, {block: "#zone", relation: "inside", anchor: "top-left-corner"} for into a container's corner, {block: "#zone", relation: "inside"} for centred in a container) or {between: [id1, id2]}. Omit to append below existing canvas content. Every anchor clears the sides it names by the two blocks' own margins, so spacing matches the rest of the diagram: an edge places the content beside that edge and centred on it, a corner places it diagonally clear of both sides it names, and naming no anchor at all centres it (which is why that needs relation "inside"; to sit beside a block, name an edge or a corner). This is one-shot drop-target vocabulary, not the enduring placement grammar, despite the shared edge and corner spellings: `end` resolves to a coordinate at insert time and manages nothing afterwards (the placement grammar has no edge-ends — a place attribute naming one is read leniently, with the end dropped and a warning). To attach content to a host rather than drop it near one, nest it under that host with place. Whatever this resolves to, the echo answers in the same frame get_diagram uses: a fragment that lands inside a container comes back nested inside it, and every pos is measured from the element enclosing it, never from the canvas. Those enclosing containers are marked existing="true" — they were already there, this insert did not make them, and they are stubs carrying geometry alone, so their own classes, labels and other children are not listed.

block.description: id of an existing block to place relative to (the '#' prefix from path refs is optional); pair with anchor and optionally relation/end

relation.description: whether the content lands within the block or beyond its border; defaults to outside. "inside" means containment, so it requires a container and errors on an icon or a text

anchor.description: a named edge or corner of the block. An edge centres the content on that edge unless an end is given; a corner names two sides and places the content diagonally clear of both. Omit it, with relation "inside", to centre the content in the block — naming no side is what centred means, which is why it is only available inside. Every gap comes from the two blocks' margins, never a fixed number

end.description: position along an edge anchor: left/right for top-edge and bottom-edge, top/bottom for left-edge and right-edge. Omit for centred; corners take no end

between.description: ids of exactly two existing blocks; the content lands centred in the gap between them. An alternative to block/relation/anchor/end, not a companion — naming both is an error

Use it to see what a collaborator changed, or to pick the seq for undo/redo. Entries at or before `baseSeq` are baked into the canonical base and can no longer be undone. Returns the most recent `limit` entries after `afterSeq`.

tools.name: list_diagrams
tools.description: List the diagrams this server can open, with their ids and titles. Use it to find the diagramId of a diagram you did not create in this conversation, or to recover one you have lost track of: nothing is remembered between calls, so an id from here or from create_diagram is the only way to name a diagram.

tools.name: create_diagram
tools.description: Create a new diagram and return its id — the diagramId every other tool takes. In a folder workspace the id is the new file's path relative to the workspace root, a .nifdi.svg named after the title, and it lasts until something moves or deletes that file; in the cloud it is an opaque id that lasts until the diagram is deleted. Keep the id: there is no current diagram, and a call that names none is rejected. list_diagrams finds it again.

tools.name: editor_url
tools.description: Return the URL of the live browser editor for a diagram (local mode), as bare text. The editor is collaborative — a user opening this URL sees the diagram live and can edit it, and their edits reach you. Nothing is opened for you: give the URL to the user to open, or navigate to it with a browser tool of your own if you have one. This is how you show a diagram to a human; to look at it yourself, call render_diagram, which returns the picture directly and needs no browser.

instructions:
nifdi-diagram edits block-and-connector diagrams: containers, text and icons wired by paths. It is a structured diagram editor, not a freeform vector or poster canvas — reach for it when the picture is boxes and arrows, and expect the server to own layout (it completes and repairs geometry rather than honouring pixel-exact composition).

The model: each block carries pos="x y" and size="w h" (space-separated numbers, both optional — omitted geometry is completed and repaired by the server) plus named style classes; a <style> block holds semicolon-separated `property: value;` rules; a <path> wires two blocks by side. Attached labels and badges are nested elements carrying a place attribute, in two categories. FULLY FIXED — place="<corner>" and place="outside-middle <edge>" — is derived wholly from the host, and each is a slot: one attachment per corner, one per edge middle. PART FIXED — place="on <edge>" (astride the border) and place="outside <edge>" (clear of it, by gap="n") — carries a free host-relative x or y along the edge and has no slot, so any number share one edge and push physics separates them. A bare place="<edge>" abbreviates outside-middle, so adding a word never silently changes a placement's category: place="bottom-edge" is the exclusive centred caption, while place="outside bottom-edge" is free along that same edge and unlimited. So <icon asset="aws:amazon-ec2"><text>Amazon EC2</text></icon> is the default caption below the icon (place="bottom-edge"), <icon asset="aws:amazon-ec2"><text place="right-edge">Amazon EC2</text></icon> sits beside its host, and <container id="mod" pos="0 0" size="320 120"><text place="on top-edge" x="120">Module</text><icon asset="iconoir:cloud" place="on top-edge" x="20"/></container> seats a title and a badge on one border by their own x. Attached blocks carry no pos — their position derives from the host, place, gap and that free coordinate. Omit pos/size and gap on a nested caption and nifdi places it automatically.
CHAINING: an attached block is itself a host, so placements nest — <container id="module" pos="0 0" size="400 120"><icon asset="iconoir:cloud" place="on bottom-edge" x="180" size="48 48"><text place="outside-middle bottom-edge">Process module</text></icon></container> straddles a container's border and carries its own caption, which no flat label can express. A nested placement may agree with its host's placement on an axis or be neutral, never oppose it; a rejection names the axis.
RECOGNISING A LABEL: text sitting beside, above or below an icon in the picture you are recreating IS that icon's label, and a name across a container's top border is that container's attached child — author both nested with place naming the side, never as a sibling text block positioned next to the host. Attachment is what makes a label travel with its host when anything moves, re-routes or reflows; a sibling is left behind. Connectors take labels the same way — the label is a <text> (or <container>) nested inside the <path>, e.g. <path><from block="#a" attach="right"/><to block="#b" attach="left"/><text>Transformed data</text></path> — and on an existing connector, set_text with the path's id creates or updates that label. A labelled connector carries its label as the path re-routes, so never fake an arrow label with a free-floating text block. Read a diagram with get_diagram and treat that canonical XML as the source of truth: accepted shorthands are normalized there, and no version attribute is needed when authoring MCP XML.

Text is markdown: a text block holds any number of lines, and headings, bullet and numbered lists, code, bold and italic are written with the usual markdown syntax, in set_text content and in <text> elements alike. Prefer one block with several lines to several one-line blocks.

Style vocabulary is semantic, not CSS: fill-colour, border-colour, text-colour, corner-radius, font-size (British -colour spelling; hex colours). CSS names like fill, stroke and color are not the property names. set_style is the most forgiving way to style — it accepts canonical semicolon declarations (commas are legacy XML compatibility only) and reports back which declarations it skipped, so prefer it over hand-writing style classes in XML when you are unsure. For incremental construction, prefer insert, connect and set_style; reserve set_diagram for full replacement.

A bare type rule (`container { … }`, `text { … }`) is how you say what the diagram's containers or texts look like: its values are shared, and a block you insert later inherits them. Every narrower rule — a `.class`, an `#id`, a descendant or child selector, `*` — is a statement about the elements it names, so its values stay on those elements: they are never folded into a bare type rule however many elements they cover, and never inherited by a block you did not name. Setting the same property through a type rule afterwards takes that scope back off.

Class names you author are preserved and re-emitted for their members while their declarations remain true of them. Where a member's value has since been changed to something the class no longer describes, the override appears as a further class after the authored name in that element's class list. All other class names are generated compression and may change freely between reads.

SEEING THE DIAGRAM: render_diagram returns the picture itself, as a PNG rendered by nifdi's own renderer. You are building something visual, and this is the only way to check that what you built looks like what you meant — layout, nesting, overlap, connector routing, colour and whether a label landed where you intended are all things the XML can be right about and the picture wrong. Render after the first few blocks land, again whenever a batch of edits completes, and once before you call the work finished; then fix what you see. Do not rasterize the augmented SVG yourself: general-purpose rasterizers (librsvg/ImageMagick/Inkscape) drop or misrender effects such as drop-shadow and rounded borders, so a PNG converted that way is not what the diagram looks like. editor_url returns a link for showing a human, not a way of looking yourself.
